abstract: Adaptive evolution is often viewed as a process through which organisms approach an increasing well-matched form for their local habitat. However, organisms must contend not only with external environments pressures but also with the internal traitors - deleterious mutations, which continuously emerge within their own genomes and is one of the determinant factors that hinders adaptation. Here, we review current strategies for identifying deleterious mutations and summarize their variation across species and populations. We then discuss the evolutionary factors that influence the persistence of deleterious mutations in natural populations. Furthermore, we examine how incorporating deleterious mutations into predictive frameworks can improve our understanding of population persistence and adaptive potential, with implications for crop breeding and biodiversity conservation. We also highlight a case study demonstrating the potential of targeted genetic modification to mitigate the effects of a deleterious mutation in tomato. Together, these perspectives underscore the importance of understanding deleterious mutations and their evolutionary dynamics for explaining and predicting adaptive evolution.
